<reason>Both sides were sharp and the debate progressed well, but PRO controlled the comparative frame the motion demands. CON's only offered rival was a confederation of "two national communities with separate political institutions," and PRO's trap in B2.1 — confederation presupposes two sovereignties — was never fully escaped. When pressed on enforcement, CON answered "Palestinian police, under Palestinian law" over sovereign Palestinian territory, which PRO credibly recast as the motion itself with residency rules attached. CON's counter (that abandoning the hard border and evacuation concedes the "content" of partition) is a clever definitional reframe, but a neutral reader is likelier to see two sovereign polities as two states than as a distinct alternative. On achievability, CON landed real damage ("eighty Gazas," a package no coalition has been offered, a map rejected three times), yet PRO's rejoinder — that placing 700,000 Israeli citizens under Palestinian criminal jurisdiction with no IDF is not the softer ask — undercuts CON's "recognition vote vs. civil war" comparison, and CON never contested that the other achievable outcomes (permanent control, cycles of war) are worse. CON's alibi argument was answered and then largely dropped. PRO's error in claiming at turn 7 that CON's Ariel answer "never came" (before CON had spoken) is a small execution blemish, corrected in the closing. Net: PRO made the decision cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2 ("who arrests the settler in Ariel?") and the follow-through in B5.1–B5.4: CON's honest answer of Palestinian police under Palestinian law let PRO argue CON had "arrived at the destination by another road," while showing the confederal ask is the same Knesset vote stripped of separation. CON's best counter was A4.5's inversion (the IDF removes settlers by force under PRO's plan) plus the "load-bearing beams are hypothetical" closing, which scored but did not dislodge the definitional capture.</best_rebuttal>
